## What Do We Mean When We Talk About Polarization?

### From Concept to Measurement to Democratic Consequences

![](./images/uma_palace.png){width="100%"}

{{< meta author >}} -- joint work with Thomas König

{{< meta date >}}

::: {.notes}
Thanks very much for having me. I am Tristan Muno, a doctoral researcher at the University of Mannheim, and this is joint work with Thomas König.

The title is a question, and I mean it as one. Over the next half hour I want to convince you that polarization is not one thing, that the way we measure it decides what we find, and that this matters for the claims people make about democracy being in danger.

I have built this for people who have not read this literature before, so please stop me if something is unclear.
:::

# Opening & Roadmap

## Hook

- Physics: polarization is the *orientation* of a wave
- Light aligned in one plane; charge pulled to two poles
- Original meaning: alignment, orientation, separation
- Nothing about conflict, hostility or pathology
- Social science supplied all three

![TODO: two panels -- unpolarized light passing through a polarizing filter and emerging aligned in one plane; alongside it a bar magnet with iron filings showing the two poles. Clean, textbook-style, no text labels needed.](./images/placeholder-physics-polarization.png){width="70%"}

::: {.notes}
Let me start somewhere that is not political science at all.

The word comes from physics, where it describes the orientation of a wave. Unpolarized light vibrates in every plane at once; you pass it through a filter and what comes out is aligned in one plane. Or think of a magnet: charge separated towards two poles.

Notice what is in that concept and what is not. What is in it is alignment, orientation, separation into poles. What is not in it is conflict. Polarized light waves are not fighting each other. There is no hostility in a magnet, and no pathology. All of that was added when the social sciences borrowed the term.

So here is the line to take away from this slide: we imported a word about alignment and turned it into a word about conflict -- and then started arguing about whether the thing is getting worse, without agreeing on what the thing is.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Agenda

Central claim: conceptual and measurement choices shape what we think we know about polarization

1. The Concept
2. From Political to Affective Polarization
3. Social Identity Theory
4. Measuring Affective Polarization
5. Empirical Insights from Europe
6. Debates on Normative Implications

::: {.notes}
Here is the route. First the concept itself, which is really a family of concepts. Then the move that dominates the field today: from asking whether positions diverge to asking how people feel about each other. Third, the theory that explains why feelings run ahead of disagreement. Fourth, measurement -- the heart of the talk. Fifth, results from a project of ours covering twenty-five European countries. And sixth, the normative debate.

The central claim, out loud: conceptual and measurement choices shape what we think we know about polarization -- and therefore what we can responsibly claim about its consequences for democracy.

And my one goal for you. By the end I want you to be suspicious of any sentence of the form "polarization is increasing" that doesn't specify *what kind*.
:::

# The Concept

## Polarization is a family of concepts

- Broadest usage: alignment, separation, sorting, divergence
- Four mathematically distinct things share the name:
  - Dispersion -- how spread out opinions are
  - Bimodality -- whether the middle is emptying out
  - Sorting -- previously independent divides become correlated
  - Distance -- how far apart group means are

![TODO: four small distributions side by side, one per concept -- (1) dispersion: a wide unimodal curve next to a narrow one; (2) bimodality: two humps with a hollow middle; (3) sorting: a scatter showing two attitudes becoming correlated; (4) distance: two curves with clearly separated means. Same axes throughout, minimal labelling.](./images/placeholder-four-distributions.png){width="85%"}

::: {.notes}
In its broadest usage, polarization refers to almost any alignment, separation, sorting or divergence. Too broad to be useful -- so, concretely, there are at least four mathematically distinct things carrying the name.

Dispersion is how spread out opinions are: take the variance, and if it grows people are further apart.

Bimodality asks whether the middle is emptying out -- whether the distribution has stopped being one hill and become two camps with a valley between.

Sorting asks whether divides that used to be independent have become correlated. If knowing your position on abortion now predicts your position on climate, and it did not thirty years ago, the public has sorted -- even if nobody has become more extreme.

Distance is about group means: how far apart the average Democrat and Republican sit.

And here is the point. These can move in opposite directions in the same dataset. A public can sort without dispersing; a distribution can spread without becoming bimodal. So "is polarization increasing?" is not one question. It is four, and they can have four different answers in the same data.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Three further axes

- Bipolar vs multipolar -- nothing requires two camps
- State vs process -- a snapshot vs a trend
- Object vs target -- who is polarized against whom?

![TODO: simple schematic contrasting a bipolar configuration (two opposed clusters on one axis) with a multipolar one (three or four clusters, ideally in two dimensions). Abstract shapes, no country or party names.](./images/placeholder-bipolar-multipolar.png){width="65%"}

::: {.notes}
Three more distinctions, quickly.

Bipolar versus multipolar. Nothing requires two camps or a single dimension -- in international relations we talk about unipolar, bipolar and multipolar orders quite happily. But polarization research grew up in the United States and often silently assumes two poles. In a European multiparty system that assumption is doing real work, and it is usually undefended.

State versus process. "Hungary is polarized" is a snapshot; "polarization is increasing" is a trend. Public debate slides between these constantly, and they have different data requirements -- for the second you need comparable measurements over time, which we often do not have.

Object versus target. Who is polarized: elites, legislators, the mass public? And against whom? Elite polarization in the US is well documented; mass polarization is contested.

So: most disagreements about polarization are disagreements about which facet people mean.

Now, how did the field actually move -- from what people think to how they feel?
:::

# From Political to Affective Polarization

## The debate on political polarization

- Originally *ideological*: divergence on issues or left-right
- Elite level: clear US congressional divergence since the 1970s
- Mass level: fiercely contested through the 2000s
- Fiorina -- better sorted, not more extreme
- Abramowitz -- genuinely polarized, especially the engaged

::: {.notes}
When political scientists first said polarization, they meant ideological polarization: divergence on issues, or on left-right.

At the elite level the evidence is clear. Look at roll-call voting in the US Congress and the parties have pulled apart steadily since the 1970s.

The fight was about the mass public. Fiorina's position [@fiorina2008polarization] was that the public is not polarized, it is better sorted: people have not moved to the extremes, they have moved to the party matching views they already held. Conservative Democrats became Republicans. The distribution barely moved -- the labels moved. Abramowitz [@abramowitz2008ispolarization] argued the opposite: it is polarized, especially among the engaged.

And notice, with the vocabulary from two slides ago, that both were partly right about different things. Fiorina is mostly claiming something about dispersion and bimodality; Abramowitz partly about sorting, and about a specific subpopulation. That stalemate is part of why the field went looking somewhere else.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Affect, not ideology

- @iyengar2012affect: ask how partisans *feel*, not where they stand
- Dislike substantially exceeds substantive disagreement
- @iyengar2015fear: partisan discrimination exceeds racial discrimination
- Two components: in-group favoritism **and** out-group animosity

> "the tendency of people identifying as \[partisans\] to view opposing partisans negatively and copartisans positively" [@iyengar2015fear; @iyengar2019origins]

![TODO: Iyengar-style over-time line plot, US, roughly 1978-2020: in-party feeling thermometer flat and high (around 70-75), out-party thermometer declining steeply (around 48 down to 20), with the widening gap shaded.](./images/placeholder-iyengar-thermometer-trend.png){width="60%"}

::: {.notes}
The move that changed the field came from Iyengar and colleagues in 2012: stop asking whether positions diverge, start asking how people feel about each other.

The striking part is what they found. Inter-partisan dislike substantially exceeds substantive disagreement -- people who barely disagree on policy can dislike each other intensely. In a much-cited follow-up, Iyengar and Westwood showed that partisan discrimination in the US, in tasks like awarding a scholarship, exceeded discrimination by race.

The definition is on the slide, and two things in it are worth flagging.

First, "people identifying as partisans." Somebody has to decide who counts. Hold that thought -- it is exactly what my own project is about.

Second, this has two components, not one: in-group favoritism and out-group animosity. Conceptually and, as we will see, empirically separable -- but a lot of writing collapses them into a single number.

The concept spread extraordinarily fast, and a big reason is the belief that it threatens democracy. But first: why would feelings run so far ahead of disagreement?
:::

# Social Identity Theory

## Why would affect exceed disagreement?

- If people disagree only moderately, why the intense dislike?
- Partisanship is not just a summary of your positions
- It is a group you belong to
- @tajfel1979integrative: categorization, identification, comparison, distinctiveness
- Self-esteem is partly bound up in the group's standing

![TODO: horizontal four-step schematic of the SIT sequence -- categorization, identification, comparison, positive distinctiveness -- as labelled arrows or chevrons, with a one-line gloss under each step.](./images/placeholder-sit-sequence.png){width="80%"}

::: {.notes}
The puzzle: if people disagree only moderately on policy, why do they dislike each other so intensely?

Social identity theory answers that partisanship is not mainly a summary of your positions. It is a group you belong to.

Tajfel and Turner describe the sequence on the slide. Categorization: the world gets sorted into us and them. Identification: you locate yourself in one of those categories and it becomes part of who you are. Comparison: you compare your group with the other. And then the motivated step, positive distinctiveness: you want that comparison to come out in your favor.

Why? Because group membership becomes part of the self-concept. Our self-esteem is partly bound up in the standing of our groups, so making my group look better relative to yours makes me feel slightly better about myself.

Notice that this mechanism does not require you to know anything about the other group's policy positions. Which raises the obvious question -- how thin can a group be before the effect disappears?
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## The minimal group paradigm

- Participants assigned to groups on a trivial pretext
- "You prefer Klee", "you prefer Kandinsky" -- often explicitly random
- No history, no contact, no stakes, no interests
- Yet allocations systematically favor the in-group [@tajfel1971social]
- **Categorization alone is enough** -- remember this

![TODO: illustration of the minimal group assignment -- a participant shown two abstract paintings, then a card reading "You are in the Klee group", and a simple allocation matrix distributing points to an anonymous in-group and out-group member.](./images/placeholder-klee-kandinsky.png){width="70%"}

::: {.notes}
The answer is: astonishingly thin.

In the classic minimal group experiments, Tajfel assigned schoolboys to groups on a completely trivial basis. In the best-known version they looked at abstract paintings and were told they preferred Klee or preferred Kandinsky. In some versions the assignment was explicitly random and participants knew it.

These groups had no history. Members never met. Nothing was at stake, nothing to fight over. They existed only as labels in the participants' heads.

And still, asked to allocate points between an anonymous in-group and an anonymous out-group member, participants systematically favored the in-group -- sometimes sacrificing absolute gain for their own group to maximize the difference between groups.

That is the finding to hold on to. Categorization alone is enough to produce discriminatory allocation: no felt attachment, no strong identity, no history required. A label suffices. We come back to this when I show you our own data.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Three implications

1. In-group love $\neq$ out-group hate [@brewer1999psychology]: in-group favoritism is the primary process, it does not require derogating out-groups. The two are empirically and conceptually separable
2. Partisanship as social identity / expressive partisanship [@huddy2015expressive]: a party is something you *are*, not just a set of positions you hold
3. Complications in multiparty Europe: who is in- and who is out-group [@rollicke2023polarisation]? Identity may span broader coalitions or camps rather than individual parties

::: {.notes}
Three implications, each of which matters later.

First, Brewer's point: in-group love is not out-group hate. Favoritism towards your own group is the primary process and it does not require derogating anybody. Which means that if your measure is a single difference score, you threw that distinction away before you started analyzing. We will decompose it later.

Second, partisanship as social identity -- expressive partisanship. A party is something you are, not just a set of positions you hold. Closer to supporting a football club than to filling in a policy questionnaire.

Third, Europe complicates this. In a two-party system the out-group is obvious. With seven parties, who is the out-group? All the others? Only the other side of the government-opposition divide? Identity may attach to camps rather than parties. This is genuinely unsettled, and it directly affects how you build any comparative measure.

Which brings us to measurement.
:::

# Measuring Affective Polarization

## The workhorse

- Feeling thermometers / like-dislike scales: rate each party 0--100
- Simplest AP measure: in-group score minus out-group score
- @reiljan2020fear -- API: in-group minus average of all out-groups
- @wagner2021affective -- Distance and Spread for multiparty settings
- Dominates because it is brief, intuitive and already fielded

![TODO: mock-up of a feeling thermometer item exactly as a respondent sees it -- "On a scale from 0 to 10, where 0 means strongly dislike and 10 means strongly like, how much do you like or dislike each of the following parties?" with a slider or radio-button grid and four generic party names.](./images/placeholder-feeling-thermometer-item.png){width="55%"}

::: {.notes}
This instrument carries almost the entire literature. A feeling thermometer, or in Europe a like-dislike scale: rate each party from 0 to 100, or 0 to 10. The slide shows what a respondent sees. The simplest measure is then a difference -- your rating of your own party minus your rating of the other one.

In multiparty systems that does not work directly, so people proposed extensions. Reiljan's Affective Polarization Index is your in-group score minus a weighted average across all out-groups. Wagner offers two alternatives: Distance, the average distance from your most-liked party, and Spread, essentially the standard deviation of your ratings.

These are not the same quantity. Distance is about how far the field is from your favorite; Spread privileges no party and does not even require you to have an in-group. Different measures, different answers -- the theme of the talk again.

Why does the thermometer dominate? Practical reasons. One item per party, the scale travels across countries, and decisively, it already sits in dozens of surveys going back decades. You can do comparative work tomorrow without collecting anything. That convenience has a price.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Two critiques that matter

1. **What is "affect"?** Like/dislike blends emotion with cognitive and instrumental evaluation, and collapses anger, fear, disgust and contempt -- emotions with very different behavioral implications [@bakker2024putting]
2. **Which target?** @druckman2019we show that when respondents are asked about "Republicans," they picture elites and activists, not the moderate neighbor who rarely discusses politics. Specify the modal partisan and estimates drop sharply

-> a large share of measured "mass animosity" may be elite animosity wearing a costume

::: {.notes}
Two critiques, both serious.

The first is about the word affect. Asking how much you like or dislike a party gives you something that blends emotion with cognitive and instrumental evaluation. When I say I dislike a party, I might mean it disgusts me, or that I have read its tax policy and think it is wrong. Not the same mental state.

And it collapses discrete emotions that behave very differently. Anger mobilizes -- angry people participate more. Fear demobilizes. Disgust and contempt go with avoidance and dehumanization. Squeezing that onto one line loses exactly the distinctions that would tell you what behavior to expect.

The second critique is even more damaging. Druckman and Levendusky asked what respondents picture when a survey says "Republicans." The answer is elites and activists -- politicians, the loudest people on television -- not the moderate neighbor who never brings politics up. Ask explicitly about ordinary voters and the estimated hostility drops sharply.

So, the uncomfortable conclusion at the bottom of the slide: a large share of measured "mass animosity" may be elite animosity wearing a costume. We may have spent a decade documenting that people dislike politicians and calling it a finding about society.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Refinements in the AP literature

- Vertical / political AP: affect toward parties and elites [@areal2024verticalvshorizontal]
- Horizontal / social AP: affect toward ordinary fellow citizens
- Vertical splits further into party AP and leader AP [@reiljan2024patterns]
- Out-parties are disliked more than their ordinary supporters
- Attitudinal self-reports vs behavioral measures

![TODO: schematic of the AP target typology -- a vertical axis running from citizen up to party and leader (vertical/political AP) crossed with a horizontal citizen-to-citizen axis (horizontal/social AP), with small icons for leader, party and voter.](./images/placeholder-vertical-horizontal-ap.png){width="65%"}

::: {.notes}
The field responded to the target problem by splitting the concept.

Vertical, or political, affective polarization is affect directed upwards, at parties and elites -- and that splits further, because how you feel about a party is not how you feel about its leader.

Horizontal, or social, affective polarization is directed sideways, at ordinary citizens who support a different party. That is what would actually constitute social division: would I mind if my daughter married one, would I hire one, would I be friends with one.

And the consistent finding is that out-parties are disliked considerably more than their ordinary supporters. So target choice does not add nuance, it changes the magnitude of the phenomenon.

One more axis, the one that matters most for what follows: attitudinal versus behavioral. Everything so far is a self-report of a feeling. That is not the same as observing what somebody does to an out-partisan when something is at stake -- and self-reports are cheap to give and cheap to exaggerate.

So what happens if we watch behavior instead?
:::

# Empirical Insights from Europe

## Data

- @hahm2024divided: cross-national conjoint experiment
- All 25 EU member states, ~29,000 respondents, fielded in 2019
- ~1,100 per country, broadly representative on key sociodemographics
- Respondents play incentivized allocation games
- Rare combination: comparative scope **and** behavioral outcomes

::: {.notes}
The data come from Hahm, Hilpert and König, published in the APSR in 2024: a cross-national conjoint experiment across all twenty-five EU member states, about twenty-nine thousand respondents, roughly eleven hundred per country, fielded in 2019, broadly representative within each country.

What makes it unusual is the combination. There is plenty of comparative survey work on affective polarization, and some very good behavioral experiments -- but those are mostly American and mostly one country at a time. Behavioral measures across twenty-five countries with a common instrument is rare, and it lets us ask whether the American findings travel.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Design

![Player 2 Profile Example. *Note:* Figure embedded from @hahm2024divided, Figure 1.](https://static.cambridge.org/binary/version/id/urn:cambridge.org:id:binary:20240123150926403-0273:S0003055423000266:S0003055423000266_fig1.png){#fig-profile}

::: {.notes}
Respondents played two classic economic games against a described co-player, and this is the profile they saw.

In the dictator game the respondent gets ten tokens and divides them between themselves and the other player. No strategy -- whatever you give away, you lose -- so what you give is a fairly clean measure of how much you care about that person. In the trust game what you send is multiplied and the other player decides how much to return, so allocation there mixes generosity with an expectation about trustworthiness.

The crucial part is the profile. The co-player is described by several attributes at once -- age, gender, occupation, party support -- randomized independently of each other. So the effect of party support on tokens received is a causal effect, cleanly separated from the rest.

And notice who the co-player is. An ordinary person, a fellow citizen. Not a party. Not a politician.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Measurement advantages

- Explicitly horizontal: the co-player is an ordinary co-national
- Non-partisan baseline condition allows decomposing AP
- In-group favoritism and out-group derogation estimated separately
- Conjoints reduce social desirability bias [@horiuchi2022does]
- Randomization identifies causal effects of attributes [@hainmueller2014causal]

::: {.notes}
Four things this buys us, mapping onto the critiques from the last section.

First, it is explicitly horizontal -- Druckman and Levendusky's objection answered by design rather than by caveat.

Second, and this is the part I like most, there is a condition where the co-player's party is simply not shown. A non-partisan baseline. So we can decompose: how much extra you give a co-partisan relative to that baseline is in-group favoritism; how much less you give an out-partisan is out-group derogation. Brewer's distinction becomes measurable rather than merely conceptual.

Third, conjoints are less prone to social desirability bias, because party is one attribute among many. Fourth, randomization means these are causal effects with well-understood estimation properties.

And the tokens are real. Nobody has to tell you how they feel.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Results I -- attitudinal AP

- Thermometer-based measures: API, Distance, Spread
- Explicit partisans -- systematically highest AP
- Implicit partisans (vote, but deny attachment) -- clearly lower
- Non-partisans -- systematically lowest
- Restricting samples to identifiers **inflates** aggregate AP

![TODO: EU25 attitudinal AP figure -- three panels (API, Distance, Spread), each plotting mean AP with credible intervals for three respondent groups: explicit partisans, implicit partisans, non-partisans. Consistent group colors across panels.](./images/placeholder-results-attitudinal-eu25.png){width="80%"}

::: {.notes}
First, what the standard attitudinal measures say, because that is the contrast case for everything after.

We split respondents into three groups. Explicit partisans say yes when asked whether they feel close to a party. Implicit partisans say no to that, but do report a party they vote for -- they have a party, they simply decline to describe themselves as attached to it. Non-partisans have neither.

We then compute affective polarization for each group using all three operationalizations from earlier -- API, Distance and Spread -- so the result cannot be an artifact of one formula.

The pattern is identical across all three. Explicit partisans systematically highest, implicit partisans clearly lower, non-partisans lowest of all.

The practical implication is the bottom line. Most comparative work restricts the sample to people who report an attachment, because that is how you identify an in-group -- but those are precisely the highest-scoring respondents. So the restriction inflates the estimate, and by different amounts in different countries, because the share reporting an attachment runs from about forty percent in some member states to over eighty in others. Your cross-country ranking is partly a ranking of how willing people are to say "yes, I feel close to a party."

Now watch what happens when we look at behavior.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Results II -- behavioral AP, pooled EU25

- Large co-partisan effects in **both** groups
- Dictator: explicit +0.99 tokens, implicit +0.93
- Contrast 0.07 -- indistinguishable from zero
- Trust: both around 1.08; contrast centered on zero
- Components (dictator): favoritism 0.54 vs 0.45, derogation 0.45 vs 0.48

![TODO: pooled EU25 behavioral figure -- coefficient plot of the co-partisan effect on tokens allocated, posterior means with credible intervals, separately for explicit and implicit partisans in the dictator and trust games; lower panel showing the explicit-minus-implicit contrast against a reference line at zero.](./images/placeholder-results-behavioral-pooled.png){width="80%"}

::: {.notes}
Start with the size of the effect, because that is the thing to see first.

In the dictator game, explicit partisans give a co-partisan about 0.99 tokens more than an out-partisan. Implicit partisans give about 0.93 more. Out of ten tokens that is substantial and clearly non-zero. Partisanship visibly changes what people do with money. In the trust game both groups sit at about 1.08. Again large, again clearly there.

So there is no question that behavioral affective polarization exists in these data -- in both groups.

The finding is what happens when you compare them. The dictator-game contrast is about 0.07 tokens, indistinguishable from zero. The trust-game contrast is centered essentially exactly on zero. The credible intervals overlap throughout.

The decomposition says the same. In-group favoritism is 0.54 for explicit partisans against 0.45 for implicit ones; out-group derogation 0.45 against 0.48. If anything the implicit partisans derogate marginally more, though I would not lean on that.

Let me be precise, because this is easy to overstate. The claim is not that implicit partisans show no behavioral polarization -- they show a lot. The claim is that the difference between the two groups is not there. Reporting an attachment adds essentially nothing to how discriminatingly you allocate money.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Results III -- by country, and one honest caveat

- Pattern holds across all 25 member states
- Faint tendencies in Denmark, Lithuania and Portugal
- Otherwise essentially no explicit/implicit difference anywhere
- **Caveat:** attitudinal measure is party-targeted (vertical)
- Behavioral measure is citizen-targeted (horizontal)

![TODO: country-wise figure -- 25 small panels or a horizontal dot-and-interval plot ordered by country, showing the explicit-minus-implicit contrast in the co-partisan effect with credible intervals against a reference line at zero; Denmark, Lithuania and Portugal visually identifiable.](./images/placeholder-results-behavioral-bycountry.png){width="80%"}

::: {.notes}
You might suspect a pooled result hides heterogeneity -- that the difference is real somewhere and gets averaged away. So here is every country separately.

The pattern holds across all twenty-five. There are faint tendencies in Denmark, Lithuania and Portugal, where the point estimates lean slightly away from zero, but the intervals still cover zero comfortably, and with twenty-five countries you expect a few to look like that by chance. Everywhere else, essentially no difference.

Now the caveat, and I want to state it before somebody states it for me.

The two measures do not share a target. The thermometer asks about parties -- vertical. The games ask about an ordinary fellow citizen -- horizontal. So when I show you a large gap in the attitudinal results and no gap in the behavioral ones, part of that divergence is not attitude versus behavior at all. It is party-target versus citizen-target, and in these data the two are perfectly confounded.

But notice what that concession amounts to. It is not a footnote that weakens the talk -- it is the talk. Two measures the literature treats as one construct give systematically different answers about the same people, because they point at different targets.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Our project: does reported attachment matter?

- Question: does *reported* attachment drive AP, or is the label enough?
- Implicit partisans deny attachment but report a vote
- They discriminate about as much as explicit identifiers
- Holds in both games, across all 25 countries
- A **theory test**, not a null result

::: {.notes}
Our question is a measurement question with a theoretical edge. Does reported partisan attachment actually drive affective polarization in Europe -- or is the party label alone sufficient?

It matters because of how the field builds its samples. To measure affective polarization you need an in-group, so you must decide who counts as a partisan, and the standard answer is: whoever says they feel close to a party. In Europe that item is famously unreliable -- Converse and Dupeux noticed sixty years ago that in France it seems to report the vote rather than precede it. The share saying yes varies enormously across countries. And everybody who says no gets dropped.

Our finding is that implicit partisans -- who explicitly deny feeling attached but do report a vote -- discriminate about as much as explicit identifiers, in both games, across all twenty-five countries.

The framing matters here, and this is the most important slide in the talk for me. This is a theory test, not a null result.

Remember the minimal group paradigm. Arbitrary categorization -- Klee or Kandinsky, assigned at random -- was enough to produce discriminatory allocation. If that is right, felt attachment should not be necessary for behavioral affective polarization either. A party label should suffice, exactly as an arbitrary painting label did. So our result is what an orthodox reading of social identity theory predicts -- and it cuts against the identity-strength accounts that dominate this literature, which treat intensity of attachment as the engine of the whole phenomenon. On behavior, the engine looks like categorization instead.

Three implications. There is no good reason to exclude implicit partisans from affective polarization estimates -- that drops people who behave identically and keeps the ones who report the most animus. The standard attachment item is only weakly related to discriminatory behavior: it tells you about willingness to report, not about conduct. And behavioral affective polarization looks cue- and categorization-driven.

Which raises the question everybody actually wants answered: is any of this bad for democracy?
:::

# Debates on Normative Implications

## The case for concern -- and against

- Claims: less compromise, lower institutional confidence, contested results [@finkel2020political; @kingzette2021affective]
- **Threat** -- the out-camp looks more extreme and malicious than it is
- **Politicization** -- norms applied selectively, by who benefits [@KekkonenHarteveld2025DemocraticNorms]
- Pushback: reducing animosity does not move democratic attitudes [@broockman2023doesaffective; @voelkel2023interventions]
- Guardrail case: hostility to anti-democratic parties may be healthy [@harteveld2022affective; @Melendez2021negative]

::: {.notes}
The reason this concept spread so fast is the worry that it damages democracy: that polarized citizens become less willing to compromise, lose confidence in institutions, and question the legitimacy of elections they lose.

Two mechanisms are usually offered. The first is threat. If the other camp looks more extreme and malicious than it really is -- and people wildly overestimate this -- the perceived cost of losing an election rises past what citizens will accept, and things they would otherwise reject start to look justified.

The second is politicization. Democratic norms stop being rules everybody applies and become weapons applied selectively. I am outraged by the procedural violation when the other side commits it, and remarkably relaxed when my own side does. The norm survives as rhetoric while dying as a constraint.

Now the pushback, which you should take seriously. Broockman, Kalla and Westwood successfully reduced partisan animosity in experiments -- and it did not move democratic attitudes in general. Voelkel and colleagues found much the same, although stronger interventions did reduce support for candidates who violate norms. So the causal chain from animosity to anti-democratic attitudes is much weaker than the correlational literature implies.

And then the genuinely inconvenient case. Suppose a party actually is anti-democratic. Intense dislike of it is not a pathology -- it is a guardrail, citizens doing their job. And empirically, hostility towards radical-right parties in Europe is often strongest among the most democratically committed citizens. On the standard measure that person is severely polarized. Are we really prepared to call that a problem to be fixed?
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## It depends what you mean

- Preferring your own side is ordinary politics, not pathology
- Agonistic vs antagonistic: legitimate adversary or enemy [@Westphal2025PoliticalTheory; @Mouffe2013agonistics]
- Modifiable vs tenacious AP [@TODO-modifiable-tenacious]
- Disliking a party $\neq$ withholding tokens from a neighbor
- Vertical and horizontal AP need different normative verdicts

::: {.notes}
So my answer to "is affective polarization bad for democracy" is the same as my answer to everything else today: it depends what you mean.

If affective polarization just means preferring your own side, that is ordinary partisan politics, not a pathology. Parties are supposed to favor their own agenda, and partisan attachment is what makes electoral accountability work. A public with no partisan preferences would not be a healthier democracy; it would be an unresponsive one.

Two distinctions help. The first comes from political theory, ultimately from Mouffe: agonistic versus antagonistic conflict. In agonistic conflict I treat you as a legitimate adversary -- I want to beat you at the next election and I accept your right to compete and win. In antagonistic conflict you are an enemy, to be defeated rather than outvoted. Only the second is a democratic problem, and the feeling thermometer cannot tell them apart. It returns the same low number either way.

The second is modifiable versus tenacious polarization -- whether the hostility responds to information and contact, or is entrenched and self-sustaining. Completely different policy implications, and again one number does not distinguish them.

And here is my own empirical version. Disliking a party on a thermometer and withholding tokens from a neighbor are not the same phenomenon. Only the second looks like social breakdown; the first might just be a citizen with clear preferences. Vertical and horizontal affective polarization deserve different normative verdicts, and at the moment they get the same one.

Back to the opening. I gave you four things that all get called polarization and said the disagreements are about which one people mean. The normative debate repeats that mistake one level up: several distinct phenomena, sharing one name and one alarm bell.
:::

# Takeaways

##

- Polarization is a family of concepts, not a thing
- Measurement choices are theoretical choices
- Attitudinal and behavioral AP answer different questions
- Reported attachment inflates AP without changing behavior
- Whether AP is "bad for democracy" depends on which AP you mean

::: {.notes}
Five things to take with you.

Polarization is a family of concepts, not a thing -- dispersion, bimodality, sorting, distance, and then vertical, horizontal, attitudinal, behavioral on top. Ask which one before accepting any claim.

Measurement choices are theoretical choices. Picking a thermometer over a behavioral task, or restricting your sample to self-identified partisans, is not a technical decision. It commits you, usually silently, to a theory of what partisanship is.

From our results: reported attachment strongly predicts expressed animosity and barely predicts discriminatory behavior. It inflates measured polarization without corresponding to any additional discrimination.

And whether affective polarization is bad for democracy depends entirely on which one you mean.

So, back to my promise. If you leave suspicious of any sentence of the form "polarization is increasing" that does not specify what kind -- the talk did its job. Thank you, and I am happy to take questions.
:::
